newsitem.title: UK: LME copper punches higher, bullish mood takes wing.
newsitem.headline: LME copper punches higher, bullish mood takes wing.

text.p: Copper prices snapped to fresh two-month highs on Tuesday in a hectic kerb-time rally reflecting the market's overwhelmingly bullish sentiment.

Copper had flaunted its staying power above $2,400 during the rings on the London Metal Exchange (LME) midsession, although prices had failed to extend beyond Monday's high of $2,415 despite good two-way business.
It was only shortly into the kerb that trading heated up and prices zipped up a high of $2,425, an important resistance level.
Three months metal ended just off that high at $2,423, a gain of $14 from Monday's kerb close.
"The market is bullish and the buyers are coming from all directions. Some longs were weeded out this morning and now people are ready to buy again," a trader said.
"If it can close above $2,425 we're going to see it up to $2,440," he added, referring to the high of the year hit on March 7. Above there, $2,450 and $2,470 were important levels.
Cash to threes backwardation reflected the gains by widening out to $63/$65, compared to $60/$65 on Monday.
Traders said the buying had originated from various sources, although funds did not figure noticeably in the buying frenzy.
"The funds have already done a lot of their buying in a lot of the metals already," one trader said.
"But if prices keep going higher they're going to have to either cover their shorts or establish fresh long positions."
The other industrial metals had less to show at the end of the kerb. Copper's strength helped pull them off their lows, but none of them managed to post noticeable gains.
Aluminium, which had drifted lower in the pre-market to the $1,660 support level, ticked higher during copper's rally and settled just $4 easier at $1,666.

Zinc also came off lows, settling $1 firmer at $1,336. Traders said, however, that it was probably overdone after posting big gains last week, and would have difficulty hurdling Monday's high around $1,340.
Tin and nickel were sharply lower after failing to recover much from early losses. Both had climbed on the back of copper last week and were now being stopped out, traders said.
Tin ended the kerb $120 lower at $5,870, while nickel finished down $45 at $7,790.

Flooding at the Russian port of Dudinka was delaying Russian nickel exports, but the interruptions would only last a few weeks arnd were not unusual for this time of year, said a spokesman for Russia's Norilsk Nickel.
Lead ended $5 lower at $625 after trading in a tiny range and alloy was indicated firmer at $1,525/30.
